extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent attorneys practicing interference and pre‑AIA priority disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria for establishing priority, conception, reduction to practice, suppression/abandonment, inurement, utility, and related doctrines in pre‑AIA interference proceedings (35 U.S.C. 102(g) context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antedating as reference under 37 CFR 1.131
rubrics_metrics.description: A antedates B as a reference in the context of a declaration or affidavit filed under 37 CFR 1.131 because A conceived the invention before B and actually reduced the invention to practice before B reduced the invention to practice, and did not abandon, suppress, or conceal the invention after actually reducing the invention to practice and before constructively reducing the invention to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show an actual date of invention prior to the effective date of a reference or activity applied under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 (subject to statutory bars). Example variations: A can antedate B by demonstrating conception and actual reduction to practice before B, or by showing conception and diligent actual reduction to practice even if that actual reduction was after B's reduction (coupled with diligence).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.131 does not apply in interference proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Interference practice operates to the exclusion of ex parte practice under 37 CFR 1.131; subject matter that is prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) and is subject to an interference is not open to further inquiry under 37 CFR 1.131 during the interference proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an application claim is the “same patentable invention” as a domestic patent, interference practice (not 1.131 affidavits) governs antedating. The term 'same patentable invention' includes anticipation or obviousness relative to the patent claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost interference counts are not per se statutory prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss of an interference count alone does not make its subject matter statutory prior art to the losing party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, lost count subject matter that independently qualifies as prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 may be used in 103 rejections. Note exceptions under res judicata/collateral estoppel (e.g., In re Deckler) where claims patentably indistinguishable from a lost claim may be barred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention 'made in this country' requirement (35 U.S.C. 102(g)/104)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) is available only if the invention was made in this country, except where statutory amendments (GATT/NAFTA/WTO) permit dates of invention established in member countries from specified dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts of conception, reduction to practice, and diligence must be demonstrated in the U.S. to invoke 102(g), though NAFTA/WTO rules allow certain foreign invention dates after specified effective dates to be recognized for priority purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression or concealment doctrine (35 U.S.C. 102(g) availability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) makes available as prior art the prior invention of another who has not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed it; an inventor who suppressed or concealed may lose the right to rely on an earlier actual date of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat a de facto last inventor who did not conceal as the legal first inventor, and view suppression/concealment as barring reliance on earlier actual invention dates both for priority and to avoid being treated as prior art. Failure to make the invention publicly known within a reasonable time after completion (e.g., no filing, no public disclosure, no public use) has been held to constitute suppression/concealment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of suppression or concealment from delay in filing
rubrics_metrics.description: During an interference, a hiatus or unreasonably long delay between actual reduction to practice and filing an application may give rise to an inference that the inventor suppressed or concealed the invention, preventing reliance on the earlier actual reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether delay is 'mere delay' or creates an inference is decided case‑by‑case. Examples: filing within one year of public disclosure may be reasonable; however, long unexplained delays (and other facts) can support an inference. Case law (e.g., Peeler v. Miller, Paulik v. Rizkalla) illustrates that 'mere delay' is not sufficient unless the delay is excessive or unjustified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression or concealment need not be attributed to the inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay or suppression attributable to others (e.g., an assignee or patent attorney) can give rise to an inference of suppression or concealment in an interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four‑year delays by an assignee or relatively short attorney workload delays have been treated as prima facie unreasonable in some cases; courts consider the reasons for and length of delay in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of suppression or concealment is rebuttable
rubrics_metrics.description: An inference of suppression or concealment arising from delay may be rebutted by showing renewed activity on the invention just prior to the rival’s entry and diligent filing of an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities that can rebut include efforts to perfect the invention, prepare the application, or prepare related compounds within the generic invention scope. Commercialization activities alone may not rebut the inference. Case examples: Lutzker v. Plet (rebuttal possible); Holmwood v. Cherpeck (perfecting activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment distinct from suppression or concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppression or concealment does not necessarily equal abandonment; an invention cannot be abandoned until it is first reduced to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding of suppression/concealment may not amount to abandonment that forfeits the right to a patent. Legal consequences differ; courts have separately analyzed abandonment vs suppression/concealment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception: definition and possession of the complete invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is 'the complete performance of the mental part of the inventive act'—formation in the mind of a definite and permanent idea of the complete and operative invention, sufficient to enable one skilled in the art to reduce it to practice without extensive experimentation or inventive skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception must show possession of every feature recited in the count and is usually proved by corroborating evidence. Conception requires contemporaneous recognition and appreciation of the invention. Conception of a species may or may not equate to conception of the genus; structure and method of obtaining (for, e.g., genes) may be required. In some unpredictable technologies conception and reduction to practice may occur simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Previously abandoned application not copending is evidence only of conception
rubrics_metrics.description: An abandoned application with which no subsequent application was copending serves only as evidence of conception and does not provide constructive reduction to practice benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the earlier application was abandoned and not co‑pending (and 35 U.S.C. 120 requirements are not satisfied), its filing does not constitute constructive reduction to practice; it may nonetheless be evidence of conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice: actual vs constructive
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to practice may be an actual reduction (a physical embodiment that works for its intended purpose) or a constructive reduction (filing a patent application on the claimed invention). Filing the application serves as both conception and constructive reduction to practice for the subject matter described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive reduction through filing removes the need to prove conception or actual reduction for content in the application. Actual reduction requires a tangible embodiment and proof of operation for intended purpose; the same evidence sufficient for constructive reduction may be insufficient for actual reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive reduction to practice requires compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description and enablement) and 35 U.S.C. 120
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking benefit of an earlier‑filed U.S. patent application, the earlier application must meet 35 U.S.C. 120 and 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description and enablement) for the subject matter of the interference count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof requires sufficient disclosure under 'how to make' and 'how to use' requirements. The written description must include all limitations of the count or show that missing text is necessarily and reasonably encompassed. The specification must support each positive limitation such that a person skilled in the art would give it the necessary and only reasonable construction. Generic terms can suffice for species if not patentably distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual reduction to practice: two‑prong test
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish an actual reduction to practice in an interference, a party must show (1) construction of an embodiment or performance of a process that met every element of the interference count, and (2) that the embodiment or process operated for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual reduction requires a physical or tangible form showing every element of the count; testing sufficient to demonstrate workability for intended purpose is necessary, though commercial readiness is not required. There is no doctrine of equivalents for counts—every limitation is material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing required to establish an actual reduction to practice varies with the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and extent of testing required depends on the particular facts and complexity of the invention; tests may be sufficient even if they do not duplicate all actual use conditions, provided a relationship between test conditions and intended use is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laboratory or bench tests can suffice if they reasonably relate to and demonstrate intended function; for products produced by processes, demonstration that the product is satisfactory may be required. Case law emphasizes fact‑specific analysis of testing adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice requires recognition and appreciation of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An actual reduction to practice requires contemporaneous appreciation by the inventor that the embodiment meets the invention; later recognition or reinterpretation cannot supply contemporaneous appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsequent testing may be admitted only to show an embodiment met the count, but not to retroactively establish contemporaneous appreciation. Exceptions and nuances in case law: inventor need not precisely know why it works, but must recognize that the tests were successful at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: All limitations of a count must be reduced to practice in an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: In interference proceedings every limitation of the count is material and must be shown to have been reduced to practice; there is no doctrine of equivalents for satisfying count limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to reduce any count limitation precludes reliance on actual reduction to practice for that count; the remedy may be a preliminary motion to amend a count to conform to proofs when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inurement: recognition by another may inure to inventor's benefit only if three‑prong test met
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of the invention by another can inure to the inventor's benefit only if (1) the inventor conceived the invention, (2) the inventor had an expectation that the embodiment tested would work for the intended purpose, and (3) the inventor submitted the embodiment for testing for the intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a non‑inventor recognizes utility but the inventor did not submit samples or request testing for the intended purpose, the recognition does not inure to the inventor. Case example: Genentech v. Chiron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility: known utility required at time of reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is not actually reduced to practice unless there is a known practical utility for the invention at the time of reduction to practice (except for plant and design inventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility may be shown by successful tests (human or appropriately correlated animal tests) or other evidence establishing substantial utility. Demonstrated substantial utility for any purpose can suffice if the count does not recite a particular utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable utility alone may be insufficient to establish practical utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A probable utility or a strong probability of utility does not by itself establish practical utility for reduction to practice; actual testing or the ability to 'foretell with certainty' utility is generally needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screening tests showing possible utility are often insufficient absent a reasonable correlation to asserted uses. Evidence is judged as a whole; reasonable correlation between observed properties and suggested uses can sometimes suffice, but caution is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence (header and application to priority/dates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable diligence must be shown in certain priority situations (e.g., to bridge from a point just prior to another's conception to a party's date of actual or constructive reduction to practice) to be awarded priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A may be awarded priority if A shows reasonable diligence from TD (a point just prior to B’s conception) until Ra in the absence of abandonment, suppression, or concealment. The manual treats diligence as a critical, fact‑specific requirement in contests of priority and interference practice; full details follow in the subsequent 2138.06 section.
